summary: For ages 5–7, teach recording data as an active skill: capture observations in simple tables, tally charts, and labelled drawings while events happen, then READ the record back to answer the original question. The core insight is that recording is not decoration — it captures information so it can be used later, because memory alone is unreliable. Includes a live capture activity, a read-back-and-choose practice set, and a reference scaffold, each with a distinct pedagogical purpose.
misconceptions: Thinking you can just remember it — not seeing why data must be written down as you go.
Recording after the fact from memory rather than in the moment, losing accuracy.
Treating the drawing/table as the end product ('finished!') rather than something to READ to answer the question.
Muddled tallies (miscounting, not gating fives) that can't be read back.
Inventing categories or changing headings mid-collection so the record can't be totalled.

activities.title: Live tally-and-table capture
steps: Before collecting, agree the table headings and categories (e.g. one row per minibeast type, or one row per kind of weather with one mark added each day of the week) so the record is ready to fill.

Watch a scene where events keep happening — minibeasts scuttle across a garden, or the weather changes each day for a week — and mark a tally stroke for each thing as it happens, counting as you go (cross the gate on the fifth stroke).
Add a labelled observational drawing of one thing you saw, alongside the counting table, so you have two complementary record types — a picture for what it looked like and a table/tally for how many.
When the question drops in ('which minibeast did we see most?' / 'which kind of weather did we have on the most days?'), read the answer directly off your own totals.
Say out loud how your record helps answer the question.
activities.insight: Writing it down as it happens is what makes the question answerable later; a record is something you READ to find an answer, not just something you made and finished.

activities.title: Read the record and choose how to record
steps: Look at a completed tally or table and answer questions from it: 'which was seen most?', 'how many altogether?', 'which day had no rain?'
Given a set of results to collect (e.g. counts of three kinds of leaf), choose which simple record would suit it — a tally chart, a two-column count table, or a labelled drawing — and say why.
Match given data to the best simple record type.
activities.insight: A record only works if it can be read back to answer the question, and different simple records suit different kinds of information.

activities.title: Parts of a tally chart (reference scaffold)
steps: Explore a labelled example tally chart and table: tap to reveal what each part is for — the heading row, one line per category, the gated group of five, the total.
Use this as a reference while setting up your own record in the capture activity.
activities.insight: A readable record has clear headings, one category per row, and tallies grouped in fives so they can be counted quickly.

checkQuestion: We want to find out which of these three toy cars rolls the furthest. You'll roll each car and need to keep a record so we don't forget the results. Set up a way to write down what happens, then do the rolls and record them. Afterwards, tell me how your record helps answer which car won. I'll watch.
checkAnswer: The child creates a simple organised record — a table or chart pairing each car with its distance (or a labelled tally/drawing) — records each result as they go, and can read from it to answer which car rolled furthest. The record is organised enough that the results can be compared.
